opening: Lord, meet us gently today and always
body:
The world rejected Christ because it did not truly know the Father. Therefore, those who carry His name, truth, and spirit should not expect easier treatment than He received. The statement, “No slave is greater than his master,” is spoken almost like a proverb. If the Master Himself was mocked, hated, betrayed, and crucified, then His followers should not expect universal acceptance.

Yet there is something deeply compassionate in this warning. Jesus does not say it to distance Himself from them, but to prepare them. It is spoken as honesty from a friend, almost as if He is saying, “Because you are mine, I will tell you the truth about this world.”

And perhaps this is one of the great themes of the Gospel of John: union with Christ does not remove suffering, but transforms its meaning.

The disciples may have believed that closeness to the Messiah would lead to earthly triumph, protection, or recognition. Instead, Jesus continually redirects them toward something greater: to remain in truth, love, and obedience even when the world rejects them.

So the two statements are not contradictory. “I have called you friends” speaks of intimacy with God, while “No slave is greater than his master” speaks of the cost of walking with Him. One reveals closeness. The other reveals the path.
